title: Feeding a Starter Older Than My Marriage
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] There is a jar on my counter containing a culture of flour and water that predates my marriage, my children, and, if I'm honest, most of my settled convictions about anything.
Narrator: A friend handed it to me a decade ago with a solemnity that felt, at the time, faintly absurd for what amounted to fermenting paste.
Narrator: [carefully] I've since come to understand the solemnity was entirely warranted, though it took years of feeding the thing before I grasped why.
Narrator: A starter, unlike most things I own, cannot simply be left alone. It demands, with a persistence bordering on reproach, that someone feed it regularly or watch it quietly die.
Narrator: [reflective] There have been stretches, grief mostly, and once a hospital stay, when I neglected it badly, and it forgave me each time, sluggishly, but it forgave me.
Narrator: I've wondered whether that's precisely why I've kept it going long after the novelty of homemade bread wore off entirely.

Narrator: [honestly] It asks so little, really, flour, water, a little attention, and offers in return this improbable continuity, a living thing that has outlasted several versions of who I used to be.
Narrator: I've given portions of it away to perhaps a dozen people now, each one carrying off a small, breathing fragment of a decade they weren't actually present for.
Narrator: [gently] There's something almost genealogical about it, this culture dividing and travelling into kitchens I'll never see, baked into loaves I'll never taste.
Narrator: My daughter has started asking to feed it herself, measuring flour with the exaggerated seriousness children reserve for tasks they suspect are secretly important.
Narrator: [calmly] I haven't told her yet that the jar will likely outlive me, that she'll inherit not bread exactly, but an obligation, gently disguised as a hobby.
Narrator: For now, she simply loves watching it bubble, and I let her believe, a little longer, that it's magic rather than mere patience, kept alive.

quiz.question: How old is the sourdough starter compared to the narrator's life events?
options: Older than her marriage, her children, and most of her settled convictions
Newer than her marriage
The same age as her daughter
Only a few months old
quiz.explanation: The narrator says the starter predates her marriage, children, and most of her settled convictions.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say a starter demands, unlike most things she owns?
options: Expensive equipment
Regular feeding, or it will quietly die
A large kitchen
Constant supervision by professionals
quiz.explanation: She explains a starter must be fed regularly with a persistence bordering on reproach, or it dies.

quiz.question: What happened during stretches when the narrator neglected the starter, such as during grief or a hospital stay?
options: It died permanently
She had to throw it away and start over
It forgave her each time, sluggishly
Nothing changed at all
quiz.explanation: She says the starter forgave her neglect each time, though sluggishly.

quiz.question: What has the narrator done with portions of the starter over the years?
options: Kept it entirely to herself
Sold it commercially
Thrown most of it away
Given it away to about a dozen people, each carrying off a fragment of a decade
quiz.explanation: She has given away portions to roughly a dozen people over the years.

quiz.question: What has the narrator not yet told her daughter?
options: That the jar will likely outlive her and the daughter will inherit an obligation disguised as a hobby
How to bake bread properly
That the starter is expensive
That she plans to stop baking
quiz.explanation: She hasn't told her daughter that the starter will likely outlive her, passing on an obligation disguised as a hobby.

quiz.question: What central claim does “Feeding a Starter Older Than My Marriage” develop?
options: A productive ritual can become a moral superstition.
Care for a starter models commitment across changing life seasons.
A precise request avoids turning irritation into accusation.
Insomnia becomes less hostile when unscheduled time loses its shame.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: Which evidence best supports the reasoning in “Feeding a Starter Older Than My Marriage”?
options: The narrator’s room feels more truthful after the ritual stops.
The violin conflicts with client calls rather than existing inherently as noise.
Its sluggish survival during absence complicates the idea of perfect maintenance.
Getting out of bed interrupts the cycle of resentful waiting.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: Which qualification prevents an oversimplified reading of “Feeding a Starter Older Than My Marriage”?
options: An unmade bed does not demonstrate a failed day.
Both neighbours accept that routines can be adjusted.
Wakefulness need not require a productive excuse.
Neglect during grief is not treated as moral failure.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: Which response best expresses the speaker’s stance in “Feeding a Starter Older Than My Marriage”?
options: The narrator shares portions while accepting their ongoing care needs.
She rejects a slogan that promises productivity through tidiness.
They negotiate times instead of demanding silence.
The narrator treats the night as a space to meet gracefully.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.

quiz.question: What implication follows most clearly from “Feeding a Starter Older Than My Marriage”?
options: Visible order is not a reliable measure of worth.
Inheritance can carry responsibility as well as sentiment.
Considerate boundaries protect a relationship better than vague resentment.
A changed frame can alter an experience without curing it.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s reasoning and stated limits.
